name: Bangladesh
card_headline: Bangladesh's elected BNP government faces arson and arrests ahead of Hasina's promised December return, garment wage protests and a Ganges treaty that expires on 12 December
card_summary: Tarique Rahman's BNP took power in February after an election the Awami League was barred from contesting. [1][2] Sheikh Hasina, sentenced to death in absentia a year ago, is in India and says she will return in December. [3][4] Police report arson and bomb attacks and mass arrests of Awami League members. [5][4] Wage protests have shut about 500 garment factories, fuel prices have risen three times since April, and the Ganges treaty expires on 12 December. [6][7][8]
card_local: Local sourcing is partial in this draft. bdnews24 and Prothom Alo report the year-old death sentence and police figures of 49 vehicles burned in ten days, and The Financial Express reports at least 30 injured in garment protests. [3][5][9]
card_international: AFP reports 107 arrests after the Awami League called a lockdown, and Reuters reports three fuel price rises since April and LNG shortages hitting knitwear factories. [4][7][10]
card_scholar: Crisis Group says the BNP's handling of an economic squeeze and the banned Awami League will shape the country's direction, and Carnegie says the old political economy has reasserted itself. [11][12]
context_md: Sheikh Hasina's government fell in August 2024 after a student-led uprising, and she fled to India. [13] The UN human rights office estimated that up to 1,400 people were killed between 15 July and 5 August 2024. [14] An interim government led by Muhammad Yunus ran the country until the 12 February 2026 election, the first without the Awami League. [1][13] The BNP and its allies won at least 212 seats and Tarique Rahman was sworn in as prime minister on 17 February. [2] The International Crimes Tribunal-1 sentenced Hasina to death in absentia on 17 November 2025. [3] Bangladesh has about 170 million people. [15]

sections.title: A landslide government with the Awami League barred and the July Charter only partly kept
sections.body_md:
Bangladesh held its 13th general election on 12 February 2026, the first national vote without the Awami League, which was barred from running. Turnout was 59.44 percent. The BNP and its allies won 212 seats and Jamaat-e-Islami and its allies 77, according to ISAS and Al Jazeera. [1][2] Carnegie's Avinash Paliwal gives party-level counts of 209 for the BNP, 68 for Jamaat and 6 for the National Citizens Party, so the allied and single-party figures should not be mixed. [12] In a referendum held the same day, 68.1 percent approved the July Charter, a package of constitutional and electoral reforms. [1]

Crisis Group found the vote largely free of violence or irregularities and the transfer of power smooth. [11] Odhikar, cited by CIVICUS, recorded at least 10 deaths and 497 injuries in post-election violence between 13 February and 31 March. [16] The UK Home Office's June fact-finding mission, published in October, quotes sources saying the situation has stabilised and that parties and journalists have more freedom than under the Awami League. [17] Its sources split on reforms: an NCP member of parliament said the government was ignoring the July Charter, while an NGO analyst said some reforms were kept. [17] Carnegie reports that the BNP has rejected or is reviewing parts of the Charter, including a separate Supreme Court secretariat. [12]

The Awami League ban continues. Carnegie says the BNP kept and formalised the suspension, and Crisis Group calls it unsustainable over the longer term and urges a review of cases against party activists. [12][11] Police sources told the UK mission that more than 21,000 politically motivated or false cases had been withdrawn. [17]

lenses.local: UNB, a Dhaka agency, carried Crisis Group's April assessment that how the BNP handles competing pressures will shape the country's direction. [11]
lenses.international: NPR, relaying AP, reported that voters approved the July Charter in a referendum held alongside the election. [18]
lenses.scholar: Carnegie's Paliwal calls the vote the most credible in nearly two decades and argues that the old political economy has reasserted itself under the BNP. [12]

sections.title: Hasina's death sentence cannot be carried out while she is in India, and her promised return has set off arson and arrests
sections.body_md:
On 17 November 2025 the International Crimes Tribunal-1 sentenced Sheikh Hasina to death in absentia for crimes against humanity over the 2024 crackdown on protesters, and gave former home minister Asaduzzaman Khan Kamal the same sentence. [3] The UN human rights office had estimated that up to 1,400 people were killed between 15 July and 5 August 2024. [14] A year on, bdnews24 reports that Hasina missed the 30-day appeal window and that the prosecution's appeal, which seeks death on a count that carried life, has no hearing date. [3] She rejects the charges and the proceedings. [13]

Extradition is stuck. Law Minister Md Asaduzzaman said on 14 November that Bangladesh had completed its legal obligations and the next step was India's. India's foreign ministry spokesperson, Randhir Jaiswal, called it a legal matter. [13] bdnews24 reports, citing unnamed reports, that India wants assurances of an appeal and retrial, and that the chief prosecutor rejected this on 15 November. [3] Al Jazeera notes that the extradition treaty has an exception for political cases and that some analysts see Delhi using the issue as a bargaining chip. [19]

Hasina said at an audio press conference in New Delhi on 5 August that she would return in December. Dhaka objected, and Prime Minister Tarique Rahman's first India visit was put on hold. [13][19] Police Headquarters says 49 vehicles were set on fire and cocktail bombs exploded at 59 locations between 7 and 16 November, with 33 cases and 60 arrests, and it blames banned Awami League members planning sabotage in December. [5] AFP reported 107 Awami League-linked arrests in Dhaka after Wednesday 18 November, a party call for a nationwide lockdown on 19 November, and Border Guard deployments in seven districts including Gopalganj. [4] Rahman told parliament that democratic forces must unite against the "conspiracies of the fallen, defeated fascist forces." [4] All India Radio, a state broadcaster, reported at least two deaths in separate incidents without detail, and no other source for that was found. [20] This draft found no Awami League statement explaining or denying the attacks.

lenses.local: Prothom Alo carries Police Headquarters' tally of burned vehicles and bombs and its attribution to the Awami League. [5]
lenses.international: AFP reported the lockdown call and the 107 arrests, and Business Today reported the law minister's statement that the next move rests with India. [4][13]
lenses.scholar: Carnegie notes that the death sentence has not been enforced because Hasina remains in exile in India. [12]

sections.title: Mob killings, press cases and a weakened rights commission after the vote
sections.body_md:
Ain o Salish Kendra counted at least 154 people beaten to death in mob violence from January to August 2026, according to Global Voices. [21] Odhikar recorded 33 people killed by mob lynching in April to June, and at least 41 killed and 970 injured in political violence in the same quarter, including four killed in clashes inside the BNP. [22] On 2 February the High Court asked the government to explain why its failure to prevent mob killings should not be declared unlawful, and on 27 August Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed told parliament the government had adopted a policy of zero tolerance. [21]

On the press, CPJ reported on 2 June that an Editors' Council delegation gave the government a list of 282 journalists facing politically motivated cases, and that at least 25 journalists are under International Crimes Tribunal investigation. [23] The offices of Prothom Alo and The Daily Star were attacked and set on fire during unrest in December 2025. [23] CIVICUS rates civic space as Repressed and says RSF ranked Bangladesh 152nd in its April 2026 index. It lists six arrests over social media posts between 31 March and 25 April, and reports that all five National Human Rights Commission members resigned in April, while a draft law would bar the commission from investigating the disciplined forces. [16]

On minorities, AP reported in February that the Bangladesh Hindu Buddhist Christian Unity Council counted more than 2,000 incidents of communal violence and at least 61 killings since August 2024. The interim government said most incidents were not driven by religious hostility, and AP verified neither side. [15] Police Headquarters said in July 2025 that it found no communal cause in the incidents it reviewed. [24] The fact-check section sets the two positions side by side.

lenses.local: Ain o Salish Kendra and Transparency International Bangladesh, cited by Global Voices, put the mob toll at 154 deaths from January to August and 31 to 42 deaths in March and April. [21]
lenses.international: CPJ and CIVICUS both describe limited progress on press freedom since the BNP took office. [23][16]
lenses.scholar: The UK mission's sources said political violence is localised and has declined since the election, and one rights NGO adviser noted a return to some earlier patterns, including mob violence. [17]

sections.title: Slow growth, 30.6 percent bad loans and an energy price shock
sections.body_md:
The World Bank's April update projects growth of 3.9 percent in FY26 and inflation of 8.5 percent. It puts the national poverty rate at 21.4 percent in 2025, up from 18.7 percent in 2022, and the non-performing loan ratio at 30.6 percent in December 2025. Tax revenue was below 7 percent of GDP in FY25. [25] The Bank says the Middle East conflict cut the number of people expected to leave poverty this year from 1.7 million to 0.5 million. [25] The IMF's Article IV review, concluded in January, put FY25 growth at 3.7 percent and gross reserves at $26.8 billion. [26] ISAS puts bad loans at about $52.7 billion and says interest payments take about 31 percent of domestic revenue. [1]

Energy is the new pressure. Reuters reported on 21 September that diesel rose from 115 to 135 taka a litre, after increases in April and June. The energy ministry says international fuel prices have more than doubled since March, and the state-owned Bangladesh Petroleum Corporation lost 228.76 billion taka ($1.9 billion) from March to August. [7] Reuters reported on 17 September that imported LNG supplies over 40 percent of Bangladesh's electricity and that spot LNG was near $30 per million BTU. A BKMEA survey found that 55 percent of knitwear factories had seen buyers cancel or cut orders since late August, and 78 percent had partly halted production. Power Minister Iqbal Hasan Mahmud said industrial growth was slowing. [10]

The BNP government decided in May to leave the existing IMF programme eight months early. The IMF mission chief confirmed on 3 June that Dhaka had applied for a fresh package, and Finance Minister Amir Khosru Mahmud Choudhury said in October that talks were continuing. [27] A February trade deal with the United States set the tariff at 19 percent, with a zero-tariff mechanism for some apparel made with US cotton and man-made fibre, and Dhaka agreed to purchases estimated at $15 billion of US energy over 15 years. [28]

lenses.local: The Daily Star, through Asia News Network, reported that IMF talks were continuing and that the government plans to seek about $4 billion in budget support in FY2026-27. [27]
lenses.international: Reuters reported the September fuel price rise and the LNG shortages that are hitting knitwear factories. [7][10]
lenses.scholar: Crisis Group warns that disruption linked to the Iran conflict is raising energy prices, straining reserves and threatening fertiliser supply, which could push millions back into poverty. [11]

sections.title: Garment workers demand Tk 30,000 a month against a Tk 12,500 minimum
sections.body_md:
The garment minimum wage is Tk 12,500 a month, set in the November 2023 review that raised it from Tk 8,000. Workers now demand Tk 30,000, about $240 and a 140 percent rise, plus an end to blacklisting and the release of detained colleagues. [9][6] The government formed a minimum wage board on 1 November. [9] The BGMEA reported that 529 of the 2,134 factories it surveyed in five industrial regions were disrupted on 1 November and that 987,190 workers had left their workplaces. [29] On 17 November AFP's sources said about 500 of the country's 4,500 garment factories were shut. [6]

Violence has accompanied the strikes. The Financial Express reported at least 30 injured, including seven police officers and four journalists, and an Anti-Terrorism Act case naming 21 people and about 1,500 unnamed. Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed called the unrest a "planned conspiracy" by outsiders, and a Dhaka police official said genuine workers were not involved in arson or vandalism. [9] Border Guard Bangladesh stepped up patrols with drones and body-worn cameras, and AFP notes that a "no work, no pay" provision lets owners withhold wages during stoppages. [6]

Worker and owner representatives on the board agreed that a revised structure takes effect on 1 December, with new pay from January 2027. [9] A board meeting was postponed on 16 November and rescheduled for 23 November, and the outcome of that meeting was not found. [6] RSIS puts the garment industry at about $45 billion. [30]

lenses.local: The Financial Express quotes worker and owner representatives agreeing on the 1 December timeline, while street clashes continued in Savar, Ashulia, Gazipur, Narayanganj and Mirpur. [9]
lenses.international: AFP reported that the BGMEA and BKMEA jointly called for wage talks to resume quickly. [6]
lenses.scholar: RSIS's Iftekharul Bashar writes that the government must stabilise a garment industry worth about $45 billion amid labour unrest while meeting IMF conditions. [30]

sections.title: India's visit on hold, China's visit done: how Dhaka is balancing its neighbours
sections.body_md:
Relations with India are strained. Rahman's first India visit, planned for August, was put on hold after Hasina's 5 August press conference, which Dhaka said had vitiated the atmosphere. India says it had nothing to do with the event. [19] Dhaka also objects to border fencing along the 4,096 km frontier, to rhetoric from India's ruling-party officials and to deportations it says bypass diplomatic verification. Its foreign ministry reaffirmed a "Bangladesh First" policy, and India's envoy, Dinesh Trivedi, urged both sides to move past the dispute. [19] Bangladesh has linked progress on extradition to a possible Rahman visit to India. [13]

Rahman visited China from 22 to 26 June. ISAS's Imran Ahmed counts 15 memorandums of understanding and two agreements, about $300 million in grant assistance and an agreement to explore a 2+2 dialogue between foreign and defence ministries. The Teesta project and the Mongla and Chattogram ports were discussed with no terms reported. [31] China remains the main supplier of military equipment, and Dhaka is also pursuing Turkish, French and British defence items and reportedly discussing logistics and information sharing with the United States. [31] Rahman rejects alignment with any power. [31] Crisis Group has urged Bangladesh to avoid aligning too closely with any single country or bloc. [32] ISAS also notes that a Chinese drone-plant deal drew US concerns and an offer of alternative defence systems. [1]

lenses.local: bdnews24 reports that India reportedly wants assurances that Hasina could appeal and receive a retrial, which Bangladesh's chief prosecutor rejected on 15 November. [3]
lenses.international: Al Jazeera, datelined New Delhi, reports that Dhaka is diversifying ties with the US, China and Pakistan while relations with India are strained. [19]
lenses.scholar: ISAS's Imran Ahmed says some analysts read the China visit as a strategic pivot while others see economic need and a strategy of autonomy. [31]

sections.title: The Ganges treaty expires on 12 December and July floods killed 59
sections.body_md:
The 1996 Ganges water-sharing treaty expires on 12 December and has no automatic extension clause, AFP reported on 29 October. Bangladesh says India has not responded to its request to renew it. India says river matters go through the Joint Rivers Commission, whose last technical talks were in May, and the last confirmed ministerial-level meeting was in 2022. A Teesta deal has been stalled since 2011. [8] Rashed Al Mahmud Titumir, a prime ministerial adviser who heads Bangladesh's technical committee, said Dhaka wants a new deal based on mutual benefit and respect, with climate provisions and the whole basin considered. [8] The article says Rahman may visit India before the expiry but no visit is confirmed. [8]

The UN's second situation report on the July floods and landslides, dated 23 July, counted 59 deaths in the seven most affected districts, about 1.28 million people affected, 74,479 houses damaged or destroyed and about 436,000 people needing assistance. It estimated $17.3 million in livestock and fisheries losses. [33] UNICEF says record rainfall affected 519,000 children, that no cyclone anticipatory-action trigger was activated this year, and that it had verified 20,439 high-risk households for possible cash assistance. [34]

lenses.local: AFP quoted a priest in the Barind region and a fish farmer describing a shrinking river, failed crops and falling catches. [8]
lenses.international: AFP carried both Bangladesh's request for a new treaty and India's position that talks belong with the Joint Rivers Commission. [8]

sections.title: About 1.2 million Rohingya, a 26 percent smaller appeal and an Arakan Army-run border
sections.body_md:
About 1.2 million Rohingya live in Bangladesh, mostly in 33 camps around Cox's Bazar, and about 150,000 have arrived since early 2024 as fighting spread in Rakhine State. [35][36] The UN and the government launched a $710.5 million appeal for 2026 in May, 26 percent lower than the 2025 request, targeting 1.56 million people including host communities. UNHCR said on 2 June that it was about 60 percent funded. [37][35] ORF records 2025 funding of $355 million against a $935 million appeal, with data through August 2025. [36] In 2025 about 35 percent of camp households depended entirely on food aid, and only 23 percent could earn money through cash-for-work. [37] UNICEF's 2026 appeal for Bangladesh needs $108.0 million and has a 22 percent gap. [34] Reuters reports nearly 900 Rohingya dead or missing on sea journeys in 2025, the deadliest year on record. [35]

Return is blocked. ORF's Sreeparna Banerjee writes that repatriation depends increasingly on dealings with the Arakan Army, which controls much of northern Rakhine, and that Dhaka faces a dilemma over engaging a group whose plans for the Rohingya are unclear. She reports that the BNP government said in February that Bangladesh cannot permanently absorb the Rohingya and that they may have to stay until conditions in Rakhine improve. More than 37,000 have been moved to Bhasan Char. [36] China offered help on repatriation negotiations during Rahman's June visit. [31]

lenses.local: bdnews24 reports that 98 partners, 52 of them Bangladeshi, back the appeal, with food assistance taking $247.3 million. [37]
lenses.international: Reuters quotes UNHCR calling on donors to keep supporting the Rohingya until safe return to Myanmar is possible. [35]
lenses.scholar: ORF reads the Arakan Army's handover of 73 fishermen to Bangladesh's border guard as a possible sign of pragmatic border coordination, while noting reports of discrimination and forced recruitment by the group. [36]

timeline.text: Sheikh Hasina flees to India after a student-led uprising ends her government.
The UN human rights office estimates up to 1,400 people were killed in the July to August 2024 crackdown.
The International Crimes Tribunal-1 sentences Hasina to death in absentia.
The US and Bangladesh announce a trade deal with a 19 percent tariff.
General election and July Charter referendum; the Awami League is barred.
Tarique Rahman is sworn in as prime minister.
The World Bank puts FY26 growth at 3.9 percent and the bad-loan ratio at 30.6 percent.
Crisis Group publishes a briefing on the new government's challenges.
The UN and Dhaka launch a $710.5 million Rohingya appeal, 26 percent below 2025.
Rahman begins a visit to China, signing 15 memorandums and two agreements.
UN counts 59 flood and landslide deaths and about 1.28 million people affected.
Hasina says in an audio press conference in New Delhi that she will return in December; Rahman's India visit is put on hold.
Diesel rises to 135 taka a litre, the third fuel price rise since April.
Garment workers walk out over wages and the government forms a minimum wage board.
The law minister says Bangladesh has completed its legal steps for Hasina's extradition.
Police report 49 vehicles burned and bombs at 59 locations in ten days; garment protests spread to the Dhaka highway.
The Awami League calls a nationwide lockdown; AFP reports 107 arrests in Dhaka and border guards in seven districts.

scores.coverage_basis: AFP, Reuters and AP file on Bangladesh around elections, fuel prices, garment unrest and the Rohingya, and Al Jazeera and Indian outlets follow the Hasina case closely [4][7][19]. Think-tank output from Crisis Group, Carnegie and ISAS is steady, and Dhaka outlets such as bdnews24 and Prothom Alo publish daily on these stories [11][12][31][3][5].

severity.basis: Odhikar recorded 33 mob killings and at least 41 political-violence deaths in April to June 2026, and police counted 49 vehicles burned and bombs at 59 locations in ten days in November [22][5].
About 1.2 million Rohingya depend on an appeal that was 60 percent funded in June, and the July floods affected about 1.28 million people [35][33].
An Editors' Council list names 282 journalists facing politically motivated cases, the Awami League remains banned and the rights commission's five members resigned in April [23][12][16].
Poverty rose to 21.4 percent, bad loans are 30.6 percent of the total and diesel has risen three times since April [25][7].
The UK mission's sources describe stabilisation since the election, but unrest around Hasina's promised return and the garment strikes grew in November [17][4][9].

parts.basis: China signed 15 memorandums and offered about $300 million in grants, the United States set a 19 percent tariff, and India and Dhaka are at odds over Hasina and water [31][28][19].
The garment industry is put at about $45 billion and imported LNG supplies over 40 percent of Bangladesh's power [30][10].
About 150,000 Rohingya have arrived since early 2024 and the Arakan Army controls much of northern Rakhine across the border [35][36].
Bangladesh has about 170 million people and hosts about 1.2 million Rohingya refugees [15][35].
An in-absentia death sentence against a former prime minister sits with an unresolved extradition request to India, and the Ganges treaty has no extension clause [3][8].

summary: Bangladesh matters beyond its borders through the Rohingya crisis, its garment exports and the contest between India, China and the United States for influence in Dhaka [35][30][31].
The Hasina extradition request and the expiring Ganges treaty are bilateral tests with India rather than global ones [13][8].
gi.up: A Hasina return or an Indian refusal that triggers wider unrest, a Rohingya movement across the border from Rakhine, or a collapse of garment exports.
gi.down: A renewed Ganges treaty, a settled garment wage and a repatriation arrangement for the Rohingya.

gaps: Local sourcing: only English-language Dhaka outlets were used, and several (Dhaka Tribune and Daily Star article pages) failed to open, so Bengali-language press (Prothom Alo Bangla, Ittefaq, Jugantor) was not read.

The Awami League's own account of the November arson and the 19 November lockdown was not found; the police attribution rests on Police Headquarters via one outlet, and the All India Radio report of two deaths is single-sourced and state-affiliated.
The outcome of the 23 November wage board meeting and events after 19 November are not covered.
Seat counts differ: 212 for the BNP and allies (Al Jazeera, ISAS) against 209 for the BNP alone (Carnegie); the Election Commission's final figures were not opened.
Crisis Group's April briefing was read through a UNB summary and its alignment recommendation through a headline only; the briefing itself was not opened.
The UK Home Office mission report was read only in part; its notes are individual sources' views and were not verified by the Home Office.
No 2026 report from Human Rights Watch, Amnesty International or the UN human rights office was opened, and the Hasina verdict's findings come from bdnews24 and AP.
Minority violence in 2026 rests on one AP report relaying Unity Council counts, and the police position dates from July 2025; no later government figures were found.
Current foreign exchange reserves, remittance and garment export figures for 2026 were not found; reserves cite the IMF's FY25 figure and the garment industry value comes from RSIS.
Chittagong Hill Tracts, labour rights beyond the wage dispute, climate adaptation and sea-level research were not covered; no peer-reviewed article was read.

The podcast episodes and the documentary were not listened to or watched, and one podcast length is not listed; the documentary's producer, Al Jazeera, is state-funded and the page shows no response from the people it names.

reporters.name: Zyma Islam
reporters.role: Senior Staff Correspondent, The Daily Star
reporters.bio: The Reuters Institute reported in August 2024 that she documented killings of protesters by searching social media for posts about the missing, contacting university clubs and visiting hospital morgues and graveyards.
reporters.why: Her method of matching photos of the dead to the living gave an independent count while official figures were absent.
reporters.label: Reuters Institute for the Study of Journalism

reporters.name: Somi Das
reporters.bio: Wrote the 2 June 2026 CPJ report assessing press freedom 100 days into Tarique Rahman's government.
reporters.why: The report lists the cases against journalists and CPJ's ten recommendations in one place.
reporters.label: Committee to Protect Journalists

reporters.name: Yashraj Sharma
reporters.bio: Wrote the 23 August 2026 Al Jazeera feature on why Tarique Rahman's India visit stalled.
reporters.why: The feature sets out the Hasina, border and water disputes with named scholars on both sides.
reporters.label: Al Jazeera

reporters.name: Avinash Paliwal
reporters.role: Nonresident scholar, South Asia Program, Carnegie Endowment
reporters.bio: Author of the 28 May 2026 Carnegie paper Bangladesh's Unfinished Revolution.
reporters.why: Gives party-level election results and analysis of the BNP's handling of the July Charter and the Awami League ban.
reporters.label: Carnegie Endowment

reporters.name: Naomi Hossain
reporters.role: Global Research Professor, Department of Development Studies, SOAS University of London
reporters.bio: Guest on Carnegie's Grand Tamasha podcast of 17 March 2026, discussing the Yunus interim government, Tarique Rahman's prospects, the economy and the military's role.
reporters.why: A development scholar's reading of the post-uprising transition.
reporters.label: Carnegie Endowment

reporters.name: Maksuda Akter
reporters.bio: Wrote the 27 September 2026 Global Voices article on mob violence and the institutional response in Bangladesh.
reporters.why: Collects Ain o Salish Kendra and TIB figures and two documented cases in one article.
reporters.label: Global Voices

reporters.name: Sreeparna Banerjee
reporters.role: Associate Fellow, Strategic Studies Programme, Observer Research Foundation
reporters.bio: Author of the 18 March 2026 ORF paper Repatriation in Limbo on the Rohingya, the Arakan Army and Bangladesh policy.
reporters.why: Sets out year-by-year Rohingya funding against appeals and Dhaka's dilemma over engaging the Arakan Army.
reporters.label: Observer Research Foundation

media.creator: Al Jazeera Investigates

media.why: Reconstructs the final days of Hasina's rule from audio recordings and eyewitness accounts, and was nominated for a 2026 International Emmy. Its claims are allegations and the report shows no response from those named.

factchecks.claim: Most attacks on Hindus and other minorities since August 2024 had no communal motive.
factchecks.by: Bangladesh Police Headquarters (July 2025) and the interim government; contested by the Bangladesh Hindu Buddhist Christian Unity Council and India's foreign ministry
factchecks.evidence: Police said in July 2025 that it found no communal cause in the incidents it reviewed, citing land and money disputes, robbery and family feuds. The Unity Council counted more than 2,000 incidents of communal violence and at least 61 killings since August 2024, and India's foreign ministry accused Dhaka of downplaying the pattern. AP did not verify either side, and the two sets of figures cover different periods and definitions.

sources.title: Police Headquarters: Most recent incidents involving minorities not communal
Bangladesh's Hindu minority in fear as attacks rise and a national election nears

factchecks.claim: Bangladesh has pivoted from India to China under the new government.
factchecks.by: Commentators cited by ISAS and Al Jazeera
factchecks.evidence: ISAS says some analysts read Rahman's June China visit as a strategic pivot while others see economic need and autonomy. It notes that China is the main military supplier and that 15 memorandums were signed, and also that Dhaka is pursuing Turkish, French and British defence items and reportedly talks with the United States. Rahman describes his principle as Bangladesh First. Al Jazeera reports that Dhaka is also moving closer to Pakistan.

local_md:
UNB, a Dhaka agency, carried Crisis Group's April assessment that how the BNP handles competing pressures will shape the country's direction. [11]

Prothom Alo carries Police Headquarters' tally of burned vehicles and bombs and its attribution to the Awami League. [5]

Ain o Salish Kendra and Transparency International Bangladesh, cited by Global Voices, put the mob toll at 154 deaths from January to August and 31 to 42 deaths in March and April. [21]

The Daily Star, through Asia News Network, reported that IMF talks were continuing and that the government plans to seek about $4 billion in budget support in FY2026-27. [27]

The Financial Express quotes worker and owner representatives agreeing on the 1 December timeline, while street clashes continued in Savar, Ashulia, Gazipur, Narayanganj and Mirpur. [9]

bdnews24 reports that India reportedly wants assurances that Hasina could appeal and receive a retrial, which Bangladesh's chief prosecutor rejected on 15 November. [3]

AFP quoted a priest in the Barind region and a fish farmer describing a shrinking river, failed crops and falling catches. [8]

bdnews24 reports that 98 partners, 52 of them Bangladeshi, back the appeal, with food assistance taking $247.3 million. [37]
international_md:
NPR, relaying AP, reported that voters approved the July Charter in a referendum held alongside the election. [18]

AFP reported the lockdown call and the 107 arrests, and Business Today reported the law minister's statement that the next move rests with India. [4][13]

CPJ and CIVICUS both describe limited progress on press freedom since the BNP took office. [23][16]

Reuters reported the September fuel price rise and the LNG shortages that are hitting knitwear factories. [7][10]

AFP reported that the BGMEA and BKMEA jointly called for wage talks to resume quickly. [6]

Al Jazeera, datelined New Delhi, reports that Dhaka is diversifying ties with the US, China and Pakistan while relations with India are strained. [19]

AFP carried both Bangladesh's request for a new treaty and India's position that talks belong with the Joint Rivers Commission. [8]

Reuters quotes UNHCR calling on donors to keep supporting the Rohingya until safe return to Myanmar is possible. [35]
scholar_md:
Carnegie's Paliwal calls the vote the most credible in nearly two decades and argues that the old political economy has reasserted itself under the BNP. [12]

Carnegie notes that the death sentence has not been enforced because Hasina remains in exile in India. [12]

The UK mission's sources said political violence is localised and has declined since the election, and one rights NGO adviser noted a return to some earlier patterns, including mob violence. [17]

Crisis Group warns that disruption linked to the Iran conflict is raising energy prices, straining reserves and threatening fertiliser supply, which could push millions back into poverty. [11]

RSIS's Iftekharul Bashar writes that the government must stabilise a garment industry worth about $45 billion amid labour unrest while meeting IMF conditions. [30]

ISAS's Imran Ahmed says some analysts read the China visit as a strategic pivot while others see economic need and a strategy of autonomy. [31]

ORF reads the Arakan Army's handover of 73 fishermen to Bangladesh's border guard as a possible sign of pragmatic border coordination, while noting reports of discrimination and forced recruitment by the group. [36]
